content: Patellofemoral pain syndrome (PFPS) is a prevalent knee condition, particularly affecting adolescents and young adults. It is characterized by pain located either behind the kneecap (retropatellar) or around the kneecap (peripatellar), and is often referred to as anterior knee pain. This pain is typically exacerbated by activities that place stress on the knee extensor mechanism, such as climbing stairs, squatting, running, cycling, or sitting with the knees bent for prolonged periods. Exercise therapy is frequently recommended as a treatment for this condition. The objective of this review was to evaluate the effects, both beneficial and harmful, of exercise therapy in reducing knee pain and improving knee function in individuals with PFPS. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Bone, Joint and Muscle Trauma Group Specialised Register, MEDLINE, EMBASE, PEDro, CINAHL, and AMED, as well as trial registries and conference abstracts. The search included studies up to mid-2014. The review included randomized and quasi-randomized trials that assessed the impact of exercise therapy on pain, functional ability, and recovery in adolescents and adults with PFPS. Comparisons included exercise therapy versus no treatment (control), exercise therapy versus other non-surgical interventions, and comparisons between different types of exercises or exercise programs. Data were extracted and analyzed independently by two reviewers, with outcomes categorized into short-term (≤3 months) and long-term (>3 months) measures of pain, functional ability, and recovery. A total of 31 trials involving 1,690 participants with PFPS were included in the review. The studies varied significantly in terms of participant characteristics, diagnostic criteria, and exercise interventions. Many trials were assessed as having a high risk of bias due to issues such as lack of blinding and quasi-randomized designs. The evidence was generally of very low quality, primarily due to methodological flaws and small sample sizes, leading to uncertainty about the reliability of the findings. For the comparison of exercise therapy versus no treatment (control), pooled data from five studies (375 participants) showed that exercise therapy resulted in a statistically significant reduction in pain during activity in the short term, with a mean difference (MD) of -1.46 (95% confidence interval [CI] -2.39 to -0.54). This reduction in pain was clinically meaningful, as the confidence interval included the minimal clinically important difference (MCID) of 1.3 on a 0-to-10 scale. Similar findings were observed for usual pain in the short term (two studies, 41 participants), pain during activity in the long term (two studies, 180 participants), and usual pain in the long term (one study, 94 participants). Exercise therapy also demonstrated benefits in improving functional ability. Pooled data from seven studies (483 participants) showed a standardized mean difference (SMD) of 1.10 (95% CI 0.58 to 1.63) in short-term functional ability, which, when expressed in terms of the Anterior Knee Pain Score (AKPS; 0 to 100), corresponded to an estimated MD of 12.21 points higher (95% CI 6.44 to 18.09 higher). This improvement exceeded the MCID of 10.0, indicating a clinically significant enhancement in function. Similar results were observed for long-term functional ability (three studies, 274 participants). Additionally, pooled data from two studies (166 participants) suggested that exercise therapy increased the likelihood of long-term recovery, with 88 more participants per 1,000 recovering compared to the control group (95% CI 2 fewer to 210 more). For the comparison of hip and knee exercises versus knee exercises alone, pooled data from three studies (104 participants) indicated that combined hip and knee exercises were more effective in reducing pain during activity in the short term, with an MD of -2.20 (95% CI -3.80 to -0.60). This reduction was clinically significant. Similar findings were observed for usual pain in the short term (two studies, 46 participants). One study (49 participants) also reported a clinically significant reduction in long-term pain during activity with hip and knee exercises. However, while the evidence tended to favor hip and knee exercises for functional ability (short-term: four studies, 174 participants; long-term: two studies, 78 participants) and recovery (one study, 29 participants), the results did not conclusively demonstrate superiority over knee exercises alone. In conclusion, this review found very low-quality but consistent evidence suggesting that exercise therapy for PFPS may lead to clinically meaningful reductions in pain, improvements in functional ability, and enhanced long-term recovery. However, the evidence is insufficient to determine the most effective type of exercise therapy, and it remains unclear whether these findings are generalizable to all individuals with PFPS. There is some very low-quality evidence indicating that combined hip and knee exercises may be more effective in reducing pain than knee exercises alone. Further high-quality randomized trials are needed to address these uncertainties. Future research should prioritize identifying key questions, standardizing diagnostic criteria, and establishing consistent outcome measures to optimize study design and inform clinical practice.
